issues.description: The problem description asks students to create a final Stock attribute and initialize it in the SealSaloon constructor (instance-level initialization), but elsewhere in the text it requires the stock attribute to be static (shared across all instances). Declaring the attribute as static final means it cannot be properly initialized in the instance constructor as described. This contradiction can confuse students about where and how to declare/initialize the stock field and may lead to incorrect implementations or compilation issues when attempting to follow both instructions.
issues.suggestedFix: Clarify the intended design: either (A) make stock an instance-level final field and instruct students to initialize it in the constructor (remove the requirement that stock be static), or (B) require stock to be a static (or static final) field and update the instructions to initialize it at declaration or in a static initializer (remove the instruction to initialize it in the instance constructor). Update the problem statement accordingly so the declaration and initialization guidance are consistent.

issues.description: The problem statement and UML specify a method named checkOrderReady() to process/serve orders (and instruct orderMeal() to call it), but the solution implementation uses a method named processOrders() instead. This name/signature mismatch between spec and reference can confuse students when comparing the intended API, and may mislead them if they look at the solution for guidance.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method name consistent across problem statement and reference solution. Either rename the solution method processOrders() to checkOrderReady() (and ensure orderMeal calls it), or update the problem description and UML to use processOrders() instead of checkOrderReady(). Ensure the chosen name appears consistently in examples and instructions.

issues.description: The problem statement repeatedly refers to a method named checkOrderReady() (the method that should attempt to serve queued orders). The reference implementation instead implements this logic in a method named processOrders(), and orderMeal() calls processOrders(). This naming mismatch (checkOrderReady vs. processOrders) can confuse students: the task specification asks them to implement or call checkOrderReady(), but the solution and expected implementation use a different identifier.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the identifier consistent: rename the solution method processOrders() to checkOrderReady(), and update any internal calls (e.g., orderMeal should call checkOrderReady()). Alternatively, update the problem statement to use processOrders() everywhere if that name is preferred.
